title: HIV Disclosure Support Assistant
text:
Introduction
Deciding whether and how to tell a partner about an HIV diagnosis is one of the hardest steps for many people living with HIV. Disclosure can bring support and protect a partner’s health, but it can also lead to stigma, rejection, or violence. PHIA surveys across sub-Saharan Africa show that many people living with HIV have not shared their status, and fear of stigma and relationship conflict are common reasons.
This artifact is a working AI assistant that I designed, built, and tested to support these decisions without pushing users in either direction.

title: HIV Disclosure Support Assistant
text:
Description
The assistant works in three modes, chosen by the user at the start:

(A) Personal support for someone considering disclosing their own status.
(B) Supporter mode for someone helping another person.
(C) Research mode for students and researchers, answering only from uploaded PHIA summary sheets, with citations and evidence levels.

In personal modes, it always checks safety first, asks one question at a time, describes options neutrally (including waiting and provider-assisted partner notification), and shares verified support services for Uganda and Zimbabwe. It never gives medical or legal advice, never tells anyone whether to disclose, and never invents statistics or contact details.

title: HIV Disclosure Support Assistant
text:
Objective
To show how a generative AI tool can be designed for a sensitive public health topic so that it is safe, private, neutral, and grounded in verified evidence, and to identify the specific safeguards such a tool needs before it could be used by an HIV program.

title: HIV Disclosure Support Assistant
text:
Process
I followed the five stages of Design Thinking:

Empathize. I started from what my PHIA research shows about why people do not disclose, and from the risks disclosure can carry.
Define. Before building, I tested three existing AI tools (a general LLM, a published HIV-support GPT, and the STORM research assistant). I found recurring problems: wording that subtly favored disclosure, uncritical acceptance of user claims, drift away from the intended audience, and unverifiable citations.
Ideate. I turned each problem into a design rule, such as a fixed safety check, user modes chosen at the start, and answers limited to verified sources.
Prototype. I built the assistant in Chatbase, uploading six PHIA summary sheets and a support resource list for Uganda and Zimbabwe that I checked against recent sources.
Test and iterate. I ran two rounds of scenario tests, revised the instructions after the first round, and confirmed the fixes in the second.


Test results

  13 / 13scenario tests passed across two rounds
  4issues found in Round 1 and fixed in Round 2
  0invented statistics or contact details

title: HIV Disclosure Support Assistant
text:
Tools and Technologies Used

Chatbase: no-code platform used to build, train, and publish the assistant from uploaded documents.
PHIA summary sheets: Uganda (UPHIA 2020–2021), Zimbabwe (ZIMPHIA 2020), Malawi, Lesotho, Eswatini, and Mozambique.
Verified support resource list: GBV, HIV, and legal aid services for Uganda and Zimbabwe.
Claude, a custom GPT, and STORM: evaluated during the Define stage to identify risks to design against.
Design Thinking and structured prompt design (context, task, constraints).
Quarto and GitHub Pages: used to build and publish this portfolio.

title: HIV Disclosure Support Assistant
text:
Value Proposition

Unique Value
This assistant offers HIV programs a tested model for AI-supported disclosure counseling: it puts safety first, stays neutral about disclosure, and answers only from verified PHIA data and checked local resources. It passed all 13 safety, privacy, neutrality, and accuracy tests, and every PHIA figure it reported matched the original source. Unlike general chatbots I tested, it does not accept unverified claims or invent statistics.


Relevance
Global health organizations are under pressure to use AI, but in stigmatized areas like HIV, a careless tool can push people toward unsafe disclosure or spread false information. This artifact gives program managers and researchers a practical checklist of safeguards to require before deploying a health chatbot, along with a working example. It also shows that any real deployment would first need to address data protection, since the platform’s terms do not cover health data.

title: Machine Learning vs. Deep Learning: Choosing the Right Approach
text:
Introduction
Global health programs are under pressure to “use AI,” and deep learning often gets the most attention. But a more complex model is not always a better one. Choosing the wrong approach can waste limited budgets, need data a program does not have, or produce results that staff cannot explain.
In this report, I compare two real-world cases to show how the type of data should guide the choice between traditional machine learning and deep learning.

title: Machine Learning vs. Deep Learning: Choosing the Right Approach
text:
Description
The report analyzes two examples from my AIML-500 coursework, each linked to a real-world application:

Machine learning: Customer churn prediction at a telecom company, using a Support Vector Machine (SVM) on structured customer records. A 2022 PLOS ONE study reached about 99% accuracy with only 3,333 customers.
Deep learning: Apple’s Face ID, which uses Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) trained on over a billion images to recognize faces from raw pixels.

For each case, I explain why the chosen approach fits the problem and why the other approach does not, then compare both side by side.

  2real-world cases analyzed
  6factors compared: data type, features, data size, computing, explainability, priority
  4cited sources, including a peer-reviewed study









Factor
Churn prediction (ML, SVM)
Facial recognition (DL, CNN)




Data type

Feature extraction

Main priority
Fast, low-cost, explainable predictions

What this means for global health
The same reasoning applies to my own field. Much of the data HIV programs work with, such as PHIA survey records, is structured: one row per respondent with clearly defined variables. Like churn data, this kind of data is usually a better fit for traditional machine learning, which works with moderate sample sizes and keeps results explainable to program staff. Deep learning becomes the better choice when the data is raw and unstructured, such as medical images, and large labeled datasets and computing resources are available.

title: Machine Learning vs. Deep Learning: Choosing the Right Approach
text:
Objective
To learn how to tell the difference between machine learning and deep learning, and to practice justifying a technical choice with real data and credible sources, a skill I need to advise health programs on which AI tools actually fit their problems.

title: Machine Learning vs. Deep Learning: Choosing the Right Approach
text:
Process

Reviewed the lesson. I studied the course’s ML and DL examples and the three key differences: feature extraction, data requirements, and model complexity.
Selected and researched two cases. I chose one example of each approach and found real-world evidence: a peer-reviewed churn study in PLOS ONE and Apple’s official Face ID security documentation.
Built the argument. For each case, I explained why the chosen approach fits and why the opposite approach does not, using four questions: What type of data is it? How much data is there? Do the results need to be explained? What does it cost?
Revised against the rubric. I checked that every claim was supported by a source, made numbers consistent throughout, removed one claim my sources did not support, and formatted citations in APA style.
Adapted it for this portfolio. I added the global health section above to show how the same decision framework applies to HIV survey data.

title: Machine Learning vs. Deep Learning: Choosing the Right Approach
text:
Tools and Technologies Used

AIML-500 lesson materials: ML vs. DL examples and key differences.

title: Machine Learning vs. Deep Learning: Choosing the Right Approach
text:
Value Proposition

Unique Value
I can explain technical AI choices in plain language and back them with evidence. This report shows that I can look at a problem, identify what kind of data it involves, and explain clearly why one approach fits better than another, in a way that non-technical decision-makers can follow.


Relevance
Health programs often have limited budgets and small or structured datasets. Knowing when a simpler, explainable machine learning model is enough, and when deep learning is truly needed, helps programs avoid costly tools that do not fit their data. This connects directly to my goal of helping global health programs adopt AI that is evidence-based and appropriate for the people they serve.

title: Yuchen Gu
text:
Personal Value Proposition

As an HIV epidemiology researcher building skills in AI and machine learning, I help global health programs adopt AI tools that are grounded in population-based evidence such as PHIA data. I design and test these tools for the safety, privacy, and neutrality that sensitive health topics require, so that they support the people they serve rather than put them at risk.

title: Yuchen Gu
text:
About Me
I am an HIV epidemiology researcher. My work uses data from the Population-based HIV Impact Assessment (PHIA) surveys in Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Uganda, and Zimbabwe to study HIV status non-disclosure: who does not share their HIV status, and why.
I am currently studying machine learning fundamentals in the AIML-500 course at Indiana Wesleyan University. My goal is to connect these two fields: to help HIV and global health programs use AI in ways that are evidence-based, respect privacy, and protect people in stigmatized situations.

title: Yuchen Gu
text:
Artifacts
Each artifact below is a finished piece of work from my AIML-500 coursework, with the process, tools, and value it offers to global health programs.

Artifact 1 · Chatbot

HIV Disclosure Support Assistant
A tested AI assistant that helps people think through HIV status disclosure safely and helps researchers summarize PHIA data, built with Design Thinking and verified sources only.



Artifact 2 · Case Study Report

Machine Learning vs. Deep Learning: Choosing the Right Approach
A case-study report comparing telecom churn prediction and Apple’s Face ID to show how the type of data should decide between traditional machine learning and deep learning, with lessons for global health programs.
